name: Citrus / hesperidic colognes

card.summary: Light fragrances built on bergamot, lemon and other citrus oils that give a fresh, clean impression for daytime and summer wear.
card.note: Citrus oils are volatile and fade quickly; some can irritate skin in sensitive users.

quick.overview:
Citrus (hesperidic) colognes are fragrances where lemon, bergamot, orange, grapefruit or similar oils lead the scent. They give a bright, clean, approachable impression and are popular in warm weather.

People use them as part of grooming: a fresh scent supports a polished look and is the classic eau de Cologne style dating to 1709. The effect is on how a person is perceived by smell rather than visually.
quick.how: Typically sprayed or splashed on skin after showering, often reapplied during the day because citrus notes are light and fade faster than woody or amber scents. Many wearers keep one for summer and daytime.
quick.risks: Fragrance can irritate sensitive skin or trigger allergies. Concentrated citrus oils are generally recognised as capable of causing skin reactions in some people; labels advise patch-testing and avoiding eyes.

lead: Citrus or hesperidic colognes are fragrances dominated by citrus-fruit oils such as lemon, bergamot, orange, mandarin, lime and grapefruit, often with neroli, lavender or rosemary. They are associated with a clean, fresh, light impression and are commonly chosen for summer and daytime [1][5].

People wear them as part of grooming: a freshly showered look is completed by a scent that reads as clean and approachable. The chain is indirect and runs through smell rather than appearance, with the scent adding to how well-kept a person comes across to the people near them. The style descends from eau de Cologne, launched in Cologne in 1709 by Giovanni Maria (Johann Maria) Farina, which Wikipedia says was supplied to nearly all royal houses in Europe [1][3].

Because citrus oils are among the lightest fragrance materials, they are top notes that evaporate quickly, and Wikipedia gives typical longevity for a cologne-strength product as about 2 hours [5]. Published research on citrus oils concerns their chemistry, biological activity and safety, including phototoxicity and skin sensitisation; no study located here tests citrus colognes against attractiveness ratings [2].

angle.text: A light citrus scent is used to signal cleanliness and freshness as part of a grooming routine. It works through smell rather than visual features.

infobox: Bergamot, lemon, orange, lime, grapefruit, neroli [1]
Citrus subfamily of the Fresh family [4]
Eau de cologne about 2 to 5 percent aromatic oils [1][5]
Cologne strength about 2 hours; shorter than woody or amber scents [5]
Bergamot oil can cause light-dependent skin reactions [6][7]

paras: The classic eau de Cologne is a dilute ethanol solution (about 70 to 90 percent alcohol) with water and a small percentage of essential oils, typically 2 to 5 percent and sometimes more, centred on lemon, orange, bergamot, lime, grapefruit and neroli, with optional lavender, rosemary, thyme or petitgrain [1]. Modern citrus colognes for men often pair these top notes with musks or woods to extend wear.

In English, 'cologne' now commonly means any fragrance marketed to men, and in American usage it can also mean a lighter, cheaper version of a perfume [1]. Concentration names are imprecise and vary by house: Wikipedia lists eau de cologne at about 2 to 3 percent, eau de toilette at 5 to 15 percent and eau de parfum at 15 to 20 percent [5].

sections.h: Where citrus sits in fragrance classification
paras: Perfumers describe a scent in three stages as it dries down. Top notes are small, light molecules perceived immediately, and Wikipedia lists all citrus materials among them; heart notes follow, and base notes such as musk and amber appear around 30 minutes after application [5]. The same source calls citrus the oldest fragrance family and says its lightweight character gave rise to eau de colognes [5].

On the fragrance wheel, a classification chart associated with the perfume taxonomist Michael Edwards, citrus is a subfamily of the Fresh family, alongside aromatic, water, green and fruity subfamilies [4]. The word 'hesperidic', which fragrance writers use for citrus-fruit accords, does not appear in that article [4].

Giovanni Maria Farina (born 8 December 1685, died 25 November 1766) was an Italian perfumer from Santa Maria Maggiore who moved to Cologne in 1706 and named his first creation after his adopted city [3]. Wikipedia dates the launch of Eau de Cologne to 1709 and says a single vial cost about half a civil servant's annual salary; the Farina firm gives 17 July 1709 as its founding date and describes itself as the world's oldest perfume factory still in existence, run today by the eighth generation of the family [1][3]. Farina is said to have written that he had found a scent reminding him of an Italian spring morning [1].

After French free trade reached Cologne in 1797, many other businesses sold products as 'Eau de Cologne' [1]. Wilhelm Mülhens developed the Original Eau de Cologne 4711, named for a house number on Glockengasse, produced since at least 1799 and now owned by Mäurer & Wirtz, which bought it from Procter & Gamble in 2006 [1]. A Paris perfumery opened in 1806 by Farina's great-grandnephew was later sold to Roger & Gallet [1]. Other houses followed, including Cordon Rouge and Cordon Vert by Francois Coty (1909 and 1905) [1]. The Ottoman Empire's first local cologne, odikolon, was produced in 1882, and offering kolonya to guests remains a custom in Turkey [1]. Eau de Cologne was once believed to protect against plague because citrus scent was thought to repel fleas [1].

Fragrance is discussed alongside hygiene and grooming as an inexpensive addition to presentation. Citrus scents are chosen for their fresh, approachable character and are usually applied after showering and reapplied as the volatile top notes fade. Wearers commonly keep a citrus cologne for summer and daytime and a woody or amber scent for evenings, a pairing consistent with the longevity and wheel placement described above [4][5].

Bergamot oil, one of the most commonly used materials in perfumery and a major component of the original Eau de Cologne, causes a light-dependent skin reaction mainly because of bergapten [6]. Phytophotodermatitis, also called berloque dermatitis, occurs when such furanocoumarins on skin meet UVA light; bergamot oil causes the most severe reactions among citrus, and Eau de Cologne is linked to the condition [7]. Reactions typically start within 24 hours and peak at 48 to 72 hours, with redness, itching and sometimes blisters that can leave dark pigmentation lasting years [7]. Freund linked pigmentation from Eau de Cologne to sun exposure in 1916, and Rosenthal coined 'berloque dermatitis' in 1925 [7].

Wikipedia says psoralen from bergamot oil was used in tanning products until 1995 and was linked to melanoma cases [6]. Dermatology guidance summarised on the phytophotodermatitis page advises washing skin with soap and cold water and avoiding sun for at least 48 hours after contact, and using UVA-blocking sunscreen [7]. A review of citrus essential oils covers biological activities and safety, with attention to phototoxicity and skin sensitisation [2]. Fragrance labels generally also carry warnings about eye contact and allergies.
No studies found on citrus colognes and perceived attractiveness. Related research examines citrus essential oils' biological activities and safety in general [2].

timeline.event: Giovanni Maria Farina is born in Santa Maria Maggiore.[3]
Eau de Cologne launched in Cologne; the Farina firm gives 17 July as its founding date.[1][3]
French free trade lets other makers sell products under the Cologne name.[1]
Production of Mülhens' Original Eau de Cologne 4711 under way.[1]
Jean Marie Joseph Farina opens a Paris perfumery, later sold to Roger & Gallet.[1]
Ahmet Faruk produces the Ottoman Empire's first local cologne, odikolon.[1]
Freund links pigmentation from Eau de Cologne to sun exposure.[7]
Psoralen from bergamot oil stops being used in tanning products, per Wikipedia.[6]
Mäurer & Wirtz acquires 4711 from Procter & Gamble.[1]
